sourceDesc.p: Digital image showing a typescript letter addressed to Leonard Woolf, authored and signed by Donald C. Brace. The letter has visible creases and damage along the edges.

HARCOURT, BRACE AND COMPANY, INC. Publishers 383 Madison Avenue, New York
Telephone:Eldorado 5-7920 Cable address: Harbrace, New York
Small rectangular logo inscribed with the lowercase initials "h" and "b"
<div type="letter" rend="typewritten>
February 23, 1933
Leonard Woolf, Esq. 52 Tavistock Square London, W.C.L
Dear Mr. Woolf
The manuscript of Mrs. Noolf's new book, FLUSH
Short handwritten mark above FLUSH, illegible.
, as announced in your letter of February seventh, has arrived, and I have just finished reading it. It is wholly delightful and has, we think, the promise of being very popular. People are more than usually aware of Mrs. Browning since the enormous success of the play, "The Barretts of Wimpole Street," and every one who saw the play will remember the spaniel who appeared as "Flush." It was a happy idea to write Flush's biography. Of course, I shall be glad to try to arrange for serialization. I have already communicated with Pictorial Review, and I am sending the manuscript to them today. This seems entirely suitable for serialization, and although the magazines are buying sparingly because of the heavy falling off in their advertising, there should be an ex- cellent chance of placing this.
We are preparing agreements for the book, and I will send them separately as soon as they are ready.
I hope we can arrange to publish the book nearly simaltaneously. It will take a certain amount of time to find out about serialization unless, happily, the first magazine it is offered to buys it at once. Then there will be the time required for serialization, and that will depend upon how soon the schedule of the magazine will permit them to begin it and how many install- ments they make of it. I will keep you informed, of course, but certainly serialization would make publication as early as June out of the question.
I assume that you will so ahead to set up the book, and that you will send finally corrected proofs whenever they are ready. I should like to see the illustrations you decide to use, and if Mrs. Bell is to make a wrapper for you, I should like to see that also. It might be well, at least for the American edition, if the book could have just the right sort of illus- trations. Undoubtedly, that would mean drawings. If a magazine takes it, they will illustrate it, and perhaps something good would come from that source which could also be used in the book.
Yours sincerely, Donald C. brace DCB:CMc
